name: Must Be Broadly Applicable
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The First Test: Does It Touch Everything?
lesson.summary: This section explains why "broad applicability" is the first hurdle a general-purpose technology must clear, and why quantum computing's speedups apply only to a narrow, mathematically specific set of problems.
lesson.body:
You already know that a general-purpose technology is defined by a cluster of traits that let it reshape economic life far beyond the field it was invented in. The first of those traits, and arguably the gatekeeper for all the others, is simple to state: the technology has to be useful in a very wide range of settings, not just a handful of specialized niches. This matters because the whole story of a GPT is about ripple effects spreading outward through an economy. If a technology only helps one narrow class of tasks, there is no wide surface for those ripples to spread across, no matter how impressive the technology is within its own domain.

Think about why the transistor clears this bar so easily. A transistor is, at bottom, a switch and an amplifier for electrical signals. Switching and amplifying signals turns out to be a step inside almost every electronic function you can imagine ,  memory, logic, sensing, communication. Because the underlying operation is so generic, engineers could bolt transistors onto radios, calculators, medical devices, and eventually every computer, without needing a fundamentally different transistor for each job. Broad applicability, mechanically speaking, comes from solving something so basic that it becomes a building block for countless other things.

Quantum computers do not offer that kind of generic building block. Their advantage comes from exploiting quantum mechanical structure ,  superposition and interference used to boost the probability of measuring a correct answer ,  and that structure only pays off when a problem has a very particular mathematical shape. Shor's algorithm gives a large speedup for factoring integers and related number-theory problems, which matters enormously for cryptography but is a narrow slice of computing overall. Grover's algorithm speeds up searching an unstructured list, but only quadratically, which is a modest gain rather than the exponential leap people often imagine, and it still requires a search problem framed in a specific way to apply. Quantum simulation shows real promise for modeling molecules and materials, because nature itself is quantum mechanical and a quantum computer can mirror that behavior directly. Outside of these families, ordinary classical computers remain equal or superior, and for most everyday computational tasks, quantum hardware offers nothing at all.

This is why the comparison to a specialized scientific instrument, rather than to something like the transistor, is apt. A powerful telescope or a mass spectrometer can be transformative within its field without ever becoming a general-purpose technology, because its usefulness depends entirely on the problem having a matching structure. Quantum computing looks like that: extraordinarily good at a defined set of problems with the right mathematical fingerprint, and largely irrelevant outside that set.

Keep this distinction in mind as you move forward, because the remaining GPT criteria all assume broad applicability as a starting point. If a technology cannot clear this first test, the later questions about spillover innovation and continuous improvement become secondary, since there is no wide base of adopters across which those effects could ever take hold.
